title: A design system for 40 product squads
subtitle: Building the governance model as carefully as the components
role: Head of Product Design — sponsored and staffed the systems team

summary: Stood up a design systems function from scratch inside a fast-growing healthcare platform, and the contribution model that let it survive 4x company growth.

sections.heading: The system wasn't the hard part
body: Atlas had tried to build a design system twice before I joined, and both attempts stalled — not because the components were wrong, but because adoption was voluntary and nobody owned the tradeoff between system consistency and squad velocity. My first move was organizational, not visual: get an explicit mandate and a governance model before drawing another button.

I proposed a federated model — a small central team owns primitives and tokens, embedded 'system champions' in each product area own domain-specific patterns, and every squad has a fast path to propose new components rather than fork the system quietly.

sections.heading: Token architecture before component architecture
body: We started with a three-tier token system — primitive, semantic, and component-level tokens — specifically so the visual language could evolve (a full rebrand happened 14 months in) without a component-by-component migration. That decision paid for itself directly: the rebrand touched token definitions in one place and propagated automatically.

sections.text: It's the first system here that got harder to ignore than to use.

sections.heading: Measuring adoption, not just existence
body: I pushed for adoption metrics to be visible the same way uptime is — a dashboard tracking token and component usage per squad, reviewed monthly with engineering leadership. Making adoption legible turned it from a design initiative into a shared operating metric, which is what got us through a period of 4x headcount growth without the system fragmenting again.

sections.heading: What made it stick
body: The two earlier attempts had good components and no model for who decides what goes in them. The lesson I carried forward: a design system is a governance problem wearing a component library's clothes. Solve the former and the latter gets much easier to sustain.
